source.title: CoLLM: A Unified Framework for Co-execution of LLMs Federated Fine-tuning and Inference
source.authors: Shaoyuan Huang; Xiao-Kai Wang; Na Yan; Xiao-Fei Wang; Wenyu Wang; Yan-Sha Deng

record.file_problem: The supplied text is a complete paper, but its title differs from the title in the prompt. The text itself identifies as arXiv:2604.16400v2.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures response quality during LoRA fine-tuning, but does not test whether held-out pretraining loss follows scaling power laws, whether scaling-law extrapolations work, or whether compute-optimal allocations follow a stable trend.
record.gate_note: The paper reports CE-loss and response-quality outcomes while fine-tuning and serving. These do not measure a scaling law or its predictability. The Coordinator's batch-size comparisons, goodput, JCT, and serving-system comparisons are not results on the claim's scaling behavior.
record.test_reason: CoLLM is a GPU-cluster serving system for joint LoRA inference and fine-tuning. It reports goodput, Q-goodput, GPU utilization, JCT and CE-loss-based response quality. It does not fit or test loss-versus-parameters, tokens or compute, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, architecture shape, or downstream predictability. It does not even cite the original scaling-law papers; the closest citation is McCandlish et al. on gradient noise, used for a batch-efficiency term. 'discusses' overstates the link, and 'cites_only' is the nearest enum.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that CoLLM's model sharing and coordinated orchestration improve inference goodput (up to 1.5×), quality-weighted goodput (up to 2.2×) and GPU utilization, by feeding fine-tuning gains into real-time serving.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes and evaluates a serving system for joint LoRA inference and fine-tuning; it does not implement or test a scaling-law method.

fits_no_version.finding: With shared model weights, response CE loss declines while LoRA fine-tuning runs concurrently with inference. Model Sharing has over 80% of responses above quality score 1, versus under 10% for Inference Only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concurrent LoRA fine-tuning with shared weights improves real-time inference response quality.

fits_no_version.finding: Separate fine-tuning with delayed deployment leaves 60% of responses below quality score 1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Delaying deployment of fine-tuning updates leaves inference serving an outdated model during training.

record.problems: The response-quality figure's model identity is not stated. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for these findings, and the CE-loss trend is described qualitatively rather than with numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No scaling-law results are reported. The fixed batch-size comparisons and their JCT/Q-goodput outcomes in §8.3, Fig. 12b, concern the serving/training coordinator rather than parameter, token, or compute scaling.

untested.parts: All: no extrapolation from small to large runs.
All: no architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
All: fine-tuning loss is reported over time, but there is no power-law form in any scale variable.
All: no downstream performance versus scale or pretraining loss.
All: no fitted exponents or fitting-choice comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: This is a systems paper unrelated to scaling laws, and none of its rows bear on any version. The record's 'discusses' relation is changed to 'cites_only': the paper never discusses the scaling-law claim, though strictly it does not cite the originals either. Fig. 2 notes that reload overhead grows with model size; this is a systems cost, not a loss scaling law.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from fits on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as a function of compute.
Effects of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Whether a power-law form holds in fine-tuning or other training regimes or modalities.
Predictability of downstream task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices.
